title: The core/data split is three-way, not two-way
decision: Separate core (portable, upstream-owned), project data (authored per repo), and generated artifacts (derived, committed to the project, hand-edited by no one).
rejected: A two-way core/data split.
why: The existing 'scrub' portability tier — portable procedure with stack-specific examples, hand-edited after seed — belongs to neither side. That is why --sync can only re-copy 'verbatim' files today and why workflow improvements never reach already-seeded repos. A repo boundary requires every file to land on one side; scrub files cannot. Phase 1 dissolves the tier: templates go to core, rendered output becomes generated.

title: The binding layer is a precondition for the split
decision: Do not attempt extraction before the render step exists.
rejected: Splitting first and rendering later.
why: Without mechanical rendering, every core update either overwrites project edits or freezes the core. That bind is not a scaffold-script shortcoming; it is the split failing at the tier that straddles the boundary.

title: Core is written in Go
decision: Go, single static binary.
rejected: Rust; Node; Python; bash.
why: Hard constraint: core must not drag a toolchain into consuming repos, or the framework-agnostic claim the split exists to make honest becomes false. That eliminates Node and Python before any comparison. Between Go and Rust the workload is I/O-bound glue — filesystem walking, YAML, markdown links, subprocess calls — because C6/C7 shell out to introspection commands rather than parsing types, so no performance or ecosystem argument applies. Go wins on familiarity and stdlib fit (filepath.WalkDir, os/exec, embed). Rust's real advantage is diagnostics (miette + serde_yaml giving line/column manifest errors, cf. open decision on schema validation); revisit only if cinch goes public and CLI UX becomes the differentiator.

title: Write core tooling in Go from Phase 1, inside the current repo
decision: Render step and checkers live at .agent/tools/ in Go during Phases 1 and 3; Phase 4 extraction is a file move.
rejected: Prototyping in bash or a scripting language and rewriting at extraction time.
why: Avoids writing the checker suite twice. Also forces the tooling to be real software from the start rather than accreting as shell.

title: No template engine; write a literal substituter
decision: ~30 lines of custom substitution for {{commands.check}}-style variables.
rejected: Go text/template or any third-party engine.
why: The requirement is literal substitution with no loops or conditionals. An engine buys edge cases that a 27B model has to read around, and takes away control of the undefined-variable error message. Note {{commands.check}} as specified is not valid Go template syntax anyway.

title: Generated artifacts are committed to the project repo
decision: Rendered workflows and index.md are committed, not rendered on demand.
rejected: Rendering at session start or on demand from core.
why: The runtime model must read literals with zero indirection, and a local-model session must not require core to be installed or reachable. index.md already follows this pattern under a staleness guard. The cost — diff noise on core upgrades — is arguably a feature: you see what changes in your procedures before it changes agent behaviour.

title: C2 guards both staleness and tampering
decision: Rendered files carry a 'generated — do not edit' header plus a content hash; the checker fails if a re-render does not reproduce the file.
rejected: Staleness checking alone.
why: Committed generated files invite hand-edits that the next render silently destroys. Staleness catches 'the manifest moved on'; tamper catches 'someone patched the output instead of the template'. Different failure, same file.

title: Distribution is a plain clone, not a submodule
decision: Core at ~/.cinch, version pinned in manifest.yml, render step reads from the local clone; go:embed puts templates in the binary.
rejected: Git submodule; vendoring templates into each project by default; publishing to a package registry.
why: Submodules add detached-HEAD friction for no benefit at this scale. Embedding makes the vendoring question largely moot. A published package only makes sense if cinch goes public. Vendoring to .agent/.harness-src/ pinned by commit remains available if self-contained project clones are later wanted.

title: The direction rule governs which checkers may exist
decision: Build only doc-upstream checks (doc is the spec, code conforms) and lateral checks (binding between two authored artifacts). Never doc-downstream.
rejected: Building a broad checker suite covering everything mechanically verifiable, on the mex model.
why: If a checker validates that a doc's copy of a machine-readable fact still matches, the fact should not have been copied — the derivability gate failed at write time, and the fix is deletion, not validation. mex ships eleven checkers of which most are doc-downstream: its checker suite is evidence of the design flaw it patches, and each checker is a category of duplication being policed rather than removed. This rule is what stops the checker layer becoming a maintenance burden of its own.

title: Per-domain code paths live in business doc front-matter
decision: Each business/<domain>.md declares its owning code paths in front-matter.
rejected: A domains: mapping in manifest.yml.
why: The manifest schema forbids a domains: key — the domain list is the filesystem, and a manifest copy would drift the way an inlined tree does. Front-matter keeps the mapping with the domain it describes. Needed by C10.

title: No time- or commit-based staleness thresholds
decision: Skip the '30 days / 50 commits' style warning class entirely.
rejected: Adopting mex's configurable staleness thresholds.
why: They are calibrated for teams and are the mechanism by which mex fails at scale: ten devs cross 50 commits in a day, so the tripwire fires permanently and gets disabled. On a personal repo they fire rarely enough to be noise-free but catch little. C1–C11 cover the real drift classes deterministically. Revisit only if the harness goes multi-dev.

title: Freshness is a write-time constraint, not a sync process
decision: The derivability gate becomes an explicit admission test: can an agent recover this from source? If yes, it is not written down.
rejected: Solving staleness with more frequent or smarter re-sync.
why: Content a code change can falsify should not be in the corpus at all. This is the answer to 'how do you keep this fresh when ten devs push daily' — a design constraint rather than a maintenance loop. The one residue is the semantic layer (business rules), which is non-derivable, correctly documented, and silently falsifiable by a behaviour change; that gets its own mechanism (C10 diff-coupling).

title: optimize-docs gets a deletion mandate
decision: It must remove content, not only refresh it — applying the derivability gate retroactively.
rejected: Leaving it framed purely as an anti-rot audit.
why: Rot includes content that should never have been admitted. Without a pruning pass the corpus only grows and the context-budget north star erodes silently. This is the mechanism mex lacks: GROW writes unconditionally and nothing ever deletes.

title: C8 mechanizes rule enumeration, which changes the Auditor seam
decision: Enumeration (every rule, every test) is a script; the Auditor seam becomes strong-model verification over a script-produced list.
rejected: The original split of cheap-model enumeration plus strong-model semantic verification.
why: Enumeration is not cheap-model work, it is no-model work. A script cannot produce a false checkmark; a cheap model can, and false checkmarks silently corrupt the integrity loop. The result is both cheaper and stronger than the original seam design.

title: The checker layer precedes the seam design
decision: Phase 3 before Phase 7.
rejected: The v1/review ordering, which designed seams earlier.
why: C8 changes what the Auditor seam should be. Designing the split first would bake in an enumeration pass that a script makes obsolete.

title: Extraction sits between Phase 3 and Phase 7
decision: Split after the checker layer, before the seam work.
rejected: Splitting early (before Phase 1) or late (after Phase 7).
why: Phase 1 makes it possible; Phase 2 shrinks what is being extracted from three duplicated workflows to one primitive; Phase 3 produces the component that most benefits from being shared and independently tested. Phases 1–3 and Phase 7 are the heaviest core-churn periods, and cross-repo friction is the split's main cost, so it belongs in the gap between them. Splitting earlier does not fail, it thrashes.

title: Fixture projects in core CI are the agnosticism test
decision: A toy Go repo and a toy Node repo in the cinch repo; CI renders into both and runs the checkers.
rejected: Asserting portability in the README and validating it when a second real project appears.
why: Extracting a framework from a single instance reliably produces a framework shaped like that instance, manifest or no manifest. Fixtures give a second consumer without needing a second real project and fail loudly the moment a project-specific assumption survives into core. Rate this above reuse as the reason to split.

title: Name: cinch
decision: Repo and CLI are both 'cinch'. Qualify only where a flat namespace forces it (cinch-harness on a registry, CLI stays bare). Never ship the bare word in metadata.
rejected: sinch, cynch, cincha, latigo, surcingle, jig, keelson.
why: Saddle hardware — the strap that holds the harness on — plus the second reading 'a certainty, an easy thing'. Both readings fit and cost one README line rather than a paragraph. Registry state: npm and PyPI both occupied by long-dormant packages; crates.io probably free but unverified; Homebrew is tap-namespaced and therefore moot; GitHub is owner-namespaced so no conflict. Cinch Cars Ltd holds CINCH trademark filings covering computer software, scoped to vehicle navigation — different class and market, low practical risk, not legal advice. Real cost is discoverability, not legality: the bare word is unsearchable against a brand that runs national TV campaigns.

title: Adopt an append-only event log for episodic rationale
decision: .agent/events/*.jsonl, minimal schema, append-only.
rejected: Extending the Session Handoff to carry rationale; a maintained decisions.md.
why: The handoff is state (where work stands); git holds diffs; business/ holds standing rules. None holds why a session went the way it did or what was ruled out. Append-only means no merge semantics, no rewrite path, no pruning pressure, and it cannot drift — it records what was believed at a time rather than claiming something about the present.

title: Multi-slot handoff is deferred, not designed
decision: Live with the single slot plus the event log; revisit only after Executor fan-out exists.
rejected: Designing multi-slot handoff now.
why: The handoff lives per plan file, so parallel work across two plans already has two independent slots. The single slot bites only for parallel lines within one plan — which only exists once a harness fans a plan's tasks out to sub-agents. The event log covers much of that case without branching the slot.

title: No GROW-style unconditional self-write
decision: Workflow and pattern docs are authored deliberately; nothing is emitted into memory as a side effect of finishing a task.
rejected: mex's GROW step, which writes a pattern and updates context files after every agent session.
why: An unbounded write path into memory with no admission gate and no pruning — only staleness warnings. On a weak local model it is a drift generator rather than drift control, and over months it reproduces the monolith the scaffold existed to avoid.

title: No narration or compliance contracts
decision: Compliance is verified through observable behaviour: did the session load the right manifest, run the checks, honour its context manifest.
rejected: 'AGENTS.MD initialized' emission; MANDATORY/protocol-violation framing; mex's ROUTER instruction to narrate what is being loaded.
why: All are the same proxy metric — the model can emit the string without doing the thing, and a weak local model reliably will. Threat-framing also works worse on small models than why-framing.

title: No pre-built index of the code itself
decision: Anything greppable is grepped, live. The corpus documents only what code cannot answer.
rejected: A vector index, embeddings, or a maintained summary of the codebase.
why: Precomputed copies of code go stale by construction. Anthropic reached the same conclusion for Claude Code, dropping an early RAG-plus-vector-DB approach for agentic search on staleness, security, and reliability grounds, while continuing to ship instruction-file memory. The line those two facts draw is exactly the derivability gate: no memory of derivable facts, memory of non-derivable ones.

title: No plugin system for checkers; no bash beyond the SessionStart hook
decision: Checkers are compiled in and configured by manifest data. The hook stays shell and only calls the binary.
rejected: A checker plugin API; implementing the checker suite in shell.
why: The introspection-command escape hatch is already the extensibility story; a second one makes the harness impossible to reason about. And a 400-line bash checker with YAML parsing is the debt this whole design exists to avoid.

title: A phase that modifies a workflow is not executed via that workflow
decision: Plan Phases 1 and 2 using the current plan-feature; land them; re-plan later phases with the rendered version. Same rule when the primitive is extracted and when tools move repos.
rejected: Executing phases in sequence without regard to which workflow files they are rewriting.
why: Phases 0–3 modify the workflows the executing agent is running from. Mid-Phase-1, plan-feature.md is being turned into a template and re-rendered while a session reads it. The bootstrapping hazard is invisible until it bites.

title: Multi-developer support
decision: Out of scope. The plan assumes a personal harness.
rejected: Building ownership, prose-merge, and warning-economics mechanisms now.
why: A team breaks three things currently free: doc ownership (who arbitrates a rule change), merge semantics on prose (git's line-based resolution is near-useless on rewritten paragraphs), and C10's economics (warnings firing on most commits get ignored). Worth knowing the semantic layer breaks first, not the mechanical one.

title: Rule-ID scheme and test-reference mechanism
decision: UNRESOLVED — blocks C8, C10, and every business doc.
why: Constraint: the reference from test to rule must be explicit (tag, structured comment, registry), not name-inferred. Name-matching is precisely what the semantic audit exists to avoid. An agent that picks one to keep moving will produce work that has to be redone.

title: Introspection strategy for C6/C7
decision: UNRESOLVED — blocks Phase 3.
why: Static parse of source versus a runtime command that dumps the route table and type set. Runtime is more accurate but adds a build dependency to the check.

title: Index delivery: committed file or hook-injected
decision: UNRESOLVED — affects P0.4 and C1.
why: The philosophy leaves both open. Interacts with D006 (generated artifacts committed).

title: Event log schema
decision: PROVISIONAL — this file's schema is the starting point.
why: Minimal is the constraint; a schema rich enough to need maintenance is the failure mode. Fields here: id, ts, kind, title, decision, rejected, why, refs.

title: cinch GitHub org versus personal repo
decision: UNRESOLVED — affects P4.1.
why: Org name availability unverified. Personal repo works either way since GitHub namespaces by owner.

title: Rule reference is a comment marker inside the test file
decision: A greppable comment above the test function: `// cinch:rule PROJ-014`. IDs are author-assigned, permanent, never reused, prefixed from the business doc's rule_prefix front-matter. Only rules in business/<domain>.md get IDs; philosophies in overview.md do not.
rejected: A test list in business doc front-matter; a standalone rule/test registry file; inferring the mapping from test names.
why: Deletion is self-correcting: delete the test and the marker goes with it, so C8 immediately reports the rule as uncovered. Both alternatives leave a stale entry claiming coverage that no longer exists — a false checkmark in the integrity loop, the worst failure mode in the system. Front-matter lists are also doc-downstream (D009) and reference tests by name, which is the name-matching the semantic audit exists to avoid. A comment marker needs no language parser, so core stays agnostic (D003). Side benefit: `tdd: rule-tests` becomes machine-decidable rather than a judgment call.

title: Static introspection for types, runtime for routes; core owns the output contract
decision: development.commands.introspect-types parses source (go/ast, TS declaration emit). development.commands.introspect-routes builds the router and prints its table. Core defines the JSON shape both must emit; repos implement the producers.
rejected: Static parsing for both; runtime dumps for both.
why: Struct fields are lexically present, so a static walk is exact, fast, and needs no build or environment. Route tables are constructed at runtime — loops, slices, helper functions, middleware groups — and static parsing gets them wrong in ways that are hard to notice; a route checker with silent false negatives is worse than none. Most routers enumerate (chi Walk, gin Routes, echo Routes). Cost: the route check must compile. If building the router requires a live DB or full config, that coupling is worth fixing on its own merits. Low stakes overall — this is a per-repo manifest binding, not core architecture, and different repos may answer differently.

title: The doc index is a committed generated file
decision: .agent/index.md is generated and committed; C1 compares it against a fresh in-memory generation.
rejected: Hook-injected at session start; hybrid pointer injection.
why: Consistent with D006 — generated artifacts are committed so the runtime model reads literals with no dependency on core being installed. C1 then compares two things inside the repo rather than a file against hook output.

title: Phase 3 lands in three waves
decision: C1, C2, C3, C4, C5, C9, C11 first; then C6 and C7; then C8.
rejected: Building the checker suite in numeric order or all at once.
why: The first wave is pure filesystem, YAML, and markdown — no stack adapters, no conventions to retrofit — so `cinch check` becomes green and useful early. C6/C7 need the introspection contract and per-repo producers. C8 is blocked on rule markers (D027) existing across the test suite, which is a migration, not a build.

title: cinch is created first and greenfield, not extracted at Phase 4
decision: Create the cinch repo as step one, empty, with its own minimal AGENTS.md. Port templates into it deliberately, piece by piece, with the project as its consumer from the first commit.
rejected: Building the binding layer and checkers inside the project's .agent/ and extracting them at Phase 4 (the v2 ordering).
why: D002 argued the render step must precede the split because the scrub tier cannot be separated without it. That is true of extraction — moving entangled files — and false of creation: a template authored in a repo with no project to leak from was never entangled. The decisive argument is context. The project's AGENTS.md is session-injected, so every harness-building session carried the project's domain corpus plus the old harness plus the in-flight transformation. Three concerns in one 90k window is the 'manifest feels like load everything' condition. A separate repo makes the separation structural rather than a discipline, and makes the agnosticism test continuous rather than a Phase 4 audit.

title: cinch's own docs live in cinch, not in the project's .agent/
decision: Roadmap, rationale, and the cinch decisions log move into the cinch repo. The project keeps its own events log for project-level decisions only.
rejected: Keeping .agent/analysis/cinch-roadmap.md and .agent/events/decisions.jsonl in the consuming project.
why: They are cinch's design record, not the project's. Left in place they enter the project's doc index, get loaded by project sessions, and are covered by C1 — the project's corpus paying for the harness's history. One fact, one place applies to the harness's own documentation.

title: Nothing lands in cinch that is not rendering into the project
decision: The project is cinch's consumer from the first commit. A template, checker, or manifest key is not done until it renders or runs against the real repo.
rejected: Building cinch to a design and wiring the project up afterwards.
why: The cost of creating cinch first is that it can be built speculatively, with no consumer forcing it to be right — the failure mode extraction-at-Phase-4 avoided by construction. Making the project the consumer from commit one restores that pressure and exercises the repo boundary continuously instead of testing it once.

title: Session-start signals and episodic memory are anytime tracks, not numbered phases
decision: Hook health signal, branch/plan injection, and the event log are project-side, independent, and schedulable whenever. They are removed from the numbered sequence.
rejected: Keeping them as Phase 0 items alongside the split.
why: Grouping by 'cheap and independent' is not a task boundary. Phase 0 spanned the hook, AGENTS.md, and the philosophy doc — three layers, against the one-layer atomicity rule — for no reason other than that all three were small. Phase 0 now has one goal.

title: cinch is built by a SOTA model; the 27B constraint applies to the consumer, not the build
decision: Build-side sessions assume a frontier model. Per-phase file lists are relevance filters (keep project domain material out of cinch sessions), not budget ceilings. Formal T<n> decomposition is not required for P0 and P1.
rejected: Applying the ~90k budgeting discipline to cinch development sessions.
why: The 90k constraint is a property of the runtime target that reads rendered workflows, not of the workspace where the harness is authored. Conflating them imposed decomposition overhead on sessions that do not need it. What does not change: install-time binding, literals over indirection, no template engine, and why-framing all exist for the consumer and stand unaffected. What does change: phase execution can be far less ceremonious.

title: cinch does not plan its own work with the project's plan-feature
decision: P0 and P1 are planned in-session against the roadmap section and its Exit line. From P3 onward, cinch plans with its own rendered task-primitive — it becomes the primitive's first consumer.
rejected: Running /plan-feature from the project harness to plan cinch phases.
why: Two independent failures. First, plan-feature carries the domain table, stack bindings, and test taxonomy — invoking it in a cinch session reimports exactly the project material P0 exists to separate, so the split would fail at step one. Second, it is structurally inapplicable: its Phase 1 front is domain rules plus an interaction table, and cinch is a Go CLI with no domains, no business rules, and no rules-to-tests closure. The dogfooding path is the fix — P2 extracts the domain-agnostic primitive, and cinch consuming its own render of it is both a planning workflow and the strongest portability evidence available.

title: The context north star is signal-to-noise, not budget
decision: Restate the north star: irrelevant material in the window degrades output even when it fits. Per-task context manifests are relevance filters, justified at any window size. Amend harness-philosophy.md accordingly, and move it into cinch/docs — the north stars and Foundation are portable spec, not project content.
rejected: Keeping 'context is a budget, not a count', which ties the discipline to a 90k ceiling.
why: The budget framing makes the manifest look like an artefact of a small window, so a frontier consumer appears to license loading everything. It does not: attention is finite independently of context length, and noise costs accuracy at 1M as it does at 90k. The signal-to-noise framing holds at every tier, which makes the harness dual-target by construction rather than by exception. Related correction: install-time binding was justified primarily by weak-model reliability, its weakest leg. The durable arguments are that runtime resolution makes manifest.yml a mandatory load on every workflow run at any tier, and that literals are statically checkable by C2/C3 while indirection can only be verified by watching a model resolve it.

title: Seam model tier is a manifest binding; declaration ships early
decision: Add a `seams:` section to manifest.yml declaring each seam's tier and constraints. The declaration plus its schema checker (C12) land in P1/P3; enforcement, fan-out, and permissions stay in P5.
rejected: Treating model tiering wholly as P5 harness vision, with the target tier implied by prose.
why: With tier as data, '27B everywhere', 'frontier everywhere', and mixed become three configurations of one design rather than three designs — which is what dual-targeting actually requires. Task granularity (max_task_layers) is the only knob whose right answer genuinely differs by tier; expressing it as data keeps the procedure identical across tiers. auditor: strong stays fixed regardless, because that assignment was never about the weak tier but about the cost of a false checkmark anywhere in the integrity loop. The declaration is a schema change plus a C3-style checker — cheap enough that it should not wait behind fan-out.

title: Workflows declare a compaction anchor
decision: Each workflow template declares the minimal state that must survive a mid-session summarization event: current task ID, its context manifest, and the completion ritual. Re-injected after compaction rather than reconstructed from a summary.
rejected: Relying on the Session Handoff, which covers cold resume between sessions.
why: A short local-model session simply ends. A frontier agent runs hundreds of tool calls and compacts its own context mid-session, summarizing away the workflow instructions it loaded at the start — a failure mode with no equivalent in the 90k design and nothing in the plan covering it. Cheap to add while the primitive is being written; expensive to retrofit into every template afterwards. Related: frontier harnesses spawn parallel sub-agents natively, so Executor fan-out and the multi-slot handoff question (D020) arrive earlier than the roadmap assumes.

title: Manifest command keys are kebab-case
decision: All development.commands keys use kebab-case, matching the make target they wrap (test-backend: make test-backend). Templates reference commands as {{commands.<key>}}, so the naming is a contract: a template authored against the scaffold example assumes kebab keys, and a consumer manifest must align before the render step. Applied in projectX P1 session 1: snake_case ids (test_backend, start_db, docs_index, ...) realigned to kebab and the five .agent docs pointing at those keys updated.
rejected: Keeping the project's pre-harness snake_case ids, or allowing a mixed style where templates read whatever keys a consumer happened to define.
why: Templates are authored once in cinch and rendered into every consumer; a key mismatch only surfaces at render time (D005 — undefined variable is an error), which is late and noisy. Binding time is the cheap moment to align, because nothing has rendered yet. Kebab-case also removes the transliteration step between manifest key and make target, and the scaffold example — the shape templates are written against — is the authoritative spelling.

title: The consumer index generator is deleted; cinch index is the single generator
decision: In projectX, delete scripts/gen-agent-index.sh and the old Makefile docs-index recipe; the pre-commit staleness guard now verifies the index by materializing the staged tree, running cinch index on it, and diffing the result against the staged .agent/index.md blob — the same semantics as C1, so pre-commit and cinch check can never disagree.
rejected: Keeping the script as a fallback for machines without the cinch binary, or porting its extra behavior (YAML/JSON entries, analysis/ inclusion, plans/ pointer line) into cinch.
why: Two generators with different formats (header, file set, directory skips) cannot agree — they fought on the first committed index, with C1 green via cinch while the script's guard stayed red. D009 is explicit: when a doc's copy of a machine-readable fact must be validated, delete the duplication instead. The dropped entries are cinch's defined index contract (D029), not losses.

title: Staged-tree verification materializes a git repo for cinch
decision: cinch resolves paths from the git repository root (repoRoot() runs git rev-parse --show-toplevel). A consumer pre-commit guard that verifies the staged tree by checkout-indexing into a temp dir must git init that snapshot before invoking cinch — an empty repo marker is enough; cinch index only walks .agent/.
rejected: Running cinch against the working tree instead of the snapshot (defeats the point of staging verification), or adding a path-free index mode to cinch to avoid the git dependency.
why: Environmental detail with a hostile failure mode: the first attempt failed with 'cinch: not inside a git repository' and no hint that a one-line git init fixes it — exactly the kind of discovery that costs an hour on re-encounter. The guard's regenerate-and-diff semantics mirror C1 so the two guards stay in lockstep.

title: cinch versions itself with a ported one-field-per-file scheme
decision: Port project_deltadocs' versioning system (its .agent/git-conventions.md) as a single-service adaptation: version/{major,minor,patch,hotfix}.go generated consts, one field per file, formatted x.y.z[letter] computed never stored; the node bump script becomes a `cinch version show|bump <type>` subcommand; .githooks/commit-msg + post-commit auto-bump on dev/main squash-merges and amend; scripts/release.sh tags cinch-vX.Y.Z and fast-forwards dev; Makefile gains setup-hooks/version-show/version-major/release. Initialized to 0.1.0 to match the consumer's harness_version pin (D008). Version files resolve next to the binary, so `cinch version show` works from any directory — including a consumer repo comparing its pin.
rejected: Keeping scripts/update-version.js as a node script (a node dependency in a Go repo, against D003); porting the two-service split (cinch is one binary, one tag); compiling the version into the binary (show would go stale between a bump and the next build — the files stay the single source of truth); adding a manifest-pin-vs-installed-version check (deferred: C2 already catches render drift, and the roadmap's wave plan does not list it).
why: The upstream conflict rationale carries over unchanged: one field per file so a dev-branch minor/patch bump and a main-branch hotfix bump never conflict at the main->dev sync merge, and the formatted string (rewritten by both sides every bump) is never stored. Making the bump script a cinch subcommand is the port's one structural change: hooks and release call $CINCH version ... and consumers get a zero-dependency way to query the installed tool's version.

title: Operational docs live in conventions/, not docs/
decision: docs/ is reserved for the core/philosophy of cinch (ROADMAP, RATIONALE, PHILOSOPHY, decisions log). git-conventions.md moved to conventions/git-conventions.md; future files describing how the repo is run rather than what it is (git workflow, versioning, release, hooks) land in conventions/.
rejected: Keeping git-conventions.md under docs/; a docs/operational/ subdirectory (docs/ is the core namespace — a sibling folder is a cleaner split).
why: docs/ is the portable-spec namespace (roadmap P0.2) — the north stars a session must read. Operational prose (which merge message triggers which bump, how to cut a release) is reference material, not philosophy; mixing the two makes the core docs noisier to navigate and blurs what is portable spec versus how this repo happens to run.

title: Template porting conventions: vars from the scaffold contract, examples genericized
decision: A ported workflow references manifest keys via {{vars}} and nothing else; project-specific literals become vars; example tables/prose (report shapes, classification examples) stay but lose project names, using <placeholder> or manifest-driven values instead. The scaffold manifest.example.yml (D040) is the variable contract: a template may assume any key it declares — e.g. {{taxonomy.test_tiers.e2e.notes}} — because a consumer without that key gets a loud render error at bind time (D005), not a silent gap. The concrete rendered path (not the manifest key) is what lands in the consumer's workflow. Templates are also harness-neutral: no harness names (Claude Code) and no slash-command invocation syntax — workflows are agent-neutral procedures referenced by file path (.agent/workflows/<name>.md); harness entry points (slash commands, skill shims) are consumer-side, not template content.
rejected: Porting workflows verbatim and parameterizing only the obvious paths (keeps project examples like signatures.md in the template — project content crossing the boundary, against AGENTS.md); over-generalizing until the rendered output loses all concreteness.
why: Templates are authored once and rendered into every consumer; a project name inside the template is wrong in every consumer but the first. D005's undefined-variable-is-an-error makes the scaffold example a usable contract rather than a hope: templates may lean on it, and a consumer that deviates fails at render, which is the cheap moment to catch it. Examples stay in templates because they teach the procedure, but they must be shape-examples, not this-project examples. The same argument makes harness names wrong: the project's own .claude/skills/ shims already call the workflows 'the canonical, agent-neutral procedure' with the skill as 'only the Claude Code entry point', so the workflow body naming the harness contradicts the consumer's own framing. First two ports (check-rules, task-primitive) landed 2026-08-04 and render green in project_deltadocs.

title: C11 ignores links inside fenced code blocks
decision: checkLinks tracks ``` fences and skips lines between them. Placeholder links in code examples (a doc template showing [<Related> Rules](<related>.md)) are illustrative, not cross-references.
rejected: Editing the three rules.md placeholder links into non-links (the noise would return on the next doc with an example, and workflows ported later re-introduce the same pattern).
why: C11's purpose is broken cross-references in prose. Example blocks teach link *shape*; flagging them produces warnings no one can act on, so they get suppressed and real findings are drowned. Fence-skipping is the same principle as ignoring code blocks in other link checkers. Closed the three rules.md warnings.

title: Consumers bind to the dev clone until first release; ~/.cinch is a release-time distribution
decision: project_deltadocs keeps CINCH ?= $(HOME)/code/cinch/bin/cinch (the dev clone); the Makefile comment that claimed 'cloned to ~/.cinch' was fixed to describe the actual wiring and to note that a ~/.cinch distribution clone lands at first release.
rejected: Cloning ~/code/cinch to ~/.cinch now and repointing the project.
why: Two copies of the templates would drift silently: cinch resolves templates and version files next to the binary, so the project would read the stale clone's templates while future sessions edit the dev clone's — C2 compares against the same stale source and reports 'harness ok' while the two trees disagree. The dev clone is the single working tree until release.sh grows an install step (or the first tag lands); then the comment and roadmap P1 wording become true.

title: The doc index skips leading YAML front-matter
decision: firstHeading() treats a leading --- ... --- block (D010 owns: lists) as front-matter, not content, and returns the H1 below it.
rejected: Forbidding front-matter in .agent docs; making the index list front-matter fields.
why: D010 put front-matter into business docs, and the first index regeneration turned 'Categories Business Rules' into 'owns:' — the front-matter line was the first non-empty line. The index contract (D029) is H1-derived descriptions; front-matter is metadata, so skipping it is the contract being restored, not changed.

title: P1: first two workflows ported and rendering green
decision: templates/check-rules.md and templates/task-primitive.md are authored as templates, rendered into project_deltadocs workflows/, and C2-green. C5 (overview.md missing categories), C9 x2 (plans missing Status:), C11 x3 (rules.md placeholder links) closed. D010 front-matter (owns: paths) landed on all eight business docs.
why: The render pipeline is proven end-to-end on the two smallest ports; the remaining eight workflows carry project-specific data (rules.md exception table, figma-restyle component inventory) that needs a manifest or project-doc home before porting.

title: Template purity is a structural Go test, not a check.go checker or a name blocklist
decision: Added templates_test.go (TestTemplatePurity), run via go test/make test, checking templates/*.md for three structural leaks that require no maintained list: command-shaped inline-code tokens (`/word`, the exact shape of `/execute-plan`, `/rules` HANDOFF.md flags), runner-config dotdir paths (`.word/`, excluding cinch's own `.agent/` convention), and stack literals hardcoded from scaffold/manifest.example.yml's development.commands values instead of referenced as {{commands.<key>}}. Also fixed Makefile's test target, which read `go test ./... 2>/dev/null || true` and silently swallowed every failure.
rejected: A check.go C-check (C1-C12 all validate a consumer's rendered/bound state against cinch's contracts via cmdCheck(root); templates/ has no consumer-side referent since templates resolve next to the cinch binary, D047 — this validates cinch's own source, not a consumer, so it isn't part of that layer). A maintained harness-name blocklist ("Claude Code", "Cursor", ...), including a demoted warning-level variant treated as a sampling instrument: cinch has exactly one reviewer today who reads every template and would catch a name-drop directly, so a warning on something already caught is pure noise, and noise next to error-level structural checks erodes trust in the checks that matter (the failure C11 hit before D046's fence-skip fix).
why: `/plan-feature` is a leak by construction — command-invocation syntax is inherently harness-glue regardless of which tool defines it — while a harness name is only a leak by lookup against a list that can never stay complete as new tools appear. C5 already established the applicable move in this repo: don't enumerate the domain list, derive it from the filesystem. The same principle applies to commands.commands to make the stack-literal check use scaffold/manifest.example.yml as its enumeration rather than a second maintained list of banned strings. The general case — prose describing how a runner surfaces something, with no flagged token — has no structural signature and stays a human judgment call while porting; that boundary is now explicit in AGENTS.md. Revisit the blocklist rejection if cinch ever takes contributors who haven't internalized the rule the way its one current reviewer has.

title: P1: optimize-docs and execute-plan ported and rendering green
decision: templates/optimize-docs.md and templates/execute-plan.md are authored as templates, rendered into project_deltadocs workflows/, and C2-green. Neither needed a {{commands.*}} substitution (no literal make commands in either source); the port dropped the "Claude Code exposes this as..." line and every /slash-command reference (rewritten as .agent/workflows/<name>.md paths), and genericized execute-plan.md real commit-history calibration examples into a <scope> placeholder shape. TestTemplatePurity (D049) passed on first write for both.
why: Continues the render pipeline proof from E001 onto the next two smallest ports per HANDOFF port order. Four of ten workflows are now rendered output; six remain hand-authored, three of which (plan-feature, sync-docs, fix-bug) are clean per HANDOFF and next in line, with rules.md, doc-philosophy, and figma-restyle needing project-side prep first.

title: templates/ holds only portable workflow templates — no nested README
decision: Deleted templates/README.md. render.go's renderAll walks every *.md under templates/ and renders it into a consumer's .agent/workflows/, with no filename exclusion — a meta-doc placed in templates/ gets rendered as if it were a workflow. templates/README.md was also fully redundant with AGENTS.md (which already states the stack/harness rules almost verbatim), so it was a doc-downstream duplicate as well as a render bug. It had already leaked into project_deltadocs as an untracked .agent/workflows/README.md, which was removed by hand (no template = no re-render, and cmdRender does not clean up orphaned output on its own). AGENTS.md's templates/ bullet now says directory-level conventions live there, not a nested README.
rejected: A filename exclusion in render.go (skip README.md) — reintroduces a maintained-name special case into the one place (D049) that was just built to avoid needing one, and does not fix the underlying duplication with AGENTS.md.
why: templates/ is walked unconditionally by renderAll (D005-era code, predates the porting work); nothing marks a file as meta-documentation versus a workflow. The cheap, structural fix is the same move D049 already made for the purity test: don't special-case a name, remove the reason a name would need special-casing. Also fixed a stray (D050) reference in templates_test.go's TestTemplatePurity doc comment (added in the same commit as D049) that pointed at a decision never actually logged; it now correctly cites D049, whose rationale is what that comment restates.

title: scaffold/manifest.example.yml gains docs-index, start-backend, start-frontend
decision: Added three development.commands entries to scaffold/manifest.example.yml — docs-index, start-backend, start-frontend — alongside the existing check/test-*/introspect-* entries, each with the same inline-comment style, because the sync-docs and fix-bug ports needed {{commands.docs-index}}, {{commands.start-backend}}, {{commands.start-frontend}} and D045 states a template may assume any key the scaffold declares.
rejected: Leaving the scaffold example as-is and relying on the consumer's real manifest.yml already having the keys. Mechanically this works — render.go/check.go read the consumer manifest, never the scaffold example — but it lets D045's contract claim ("a template may assume any key it declares") go silently false, which templates/task-primitive.md's prior {{commands.test}} usage already did once, undetected until this session.
why: The scaffold example is the documented variable contract; a template drawing on an undeclared key is invisible drift that only a manual manifest diff would catch. Fixing it going forward is cheap (a three-line addition) and keeps the contract's own stated rule true. The pre-existing commands.test gap (task-primitive.md, never added to the scaffold example) is noted but not fixed this session — flagged here rather than repeated silently a second time.

title: P1: plan-feature, sync-docs, fix-bug ported and rendering green
decision: templates/plan-feature.md, templates/sync-docs.md, and templates/fix-bug.md are authored as templates, rendered into project_deltadocs workflows/, and C2-green, each verified individually before the next port started (D033). Slash-command and italic Claude-Code-framing lines dropped; sibling-workflow prose references rewritten as .agent/workflows/<name>.md paths; plan-feature's rule-interaction-table example and sync-docs's quirks examples genericized into placeholder shapes; fix-bug's test-backend/test-frontend table row kept as tier-cmd mapping prose (matching task-primitive.md's existing treatment of tier-derived values) while its non-tier-derived start-backend/start-frontend row became a direct {{commands.*}} substitution. One correction made mid-port: sync-docs.md's [Doc Philosophy](doc-philosophy.md) markdown link was initially rewritten to .agent/workflows/doc-philosophy.md to match the prose convention, which broke C11 (link resolution is relative to the file's own directory, so the sibling-reference convention only applies to backtick prose, not actual markdown link targets) — reverted to the original relative link, which was already correct.
why: Continues the render pipeline proof from E001/E002 onto the three workflows HANDOFF's port order named next. Seven of ten workflows are now rendered output; three remain hand-authored (rules.md, doc-philosophy, figma-restyle), each blocked on project-side prep per HANDOFF before they can port.

title: rules.md's API-resource exception table moves into business/overview.md § Structure Convention
decision: The three bullets naming api/access.md, api/auth.md, api/users.md as having no business/*.md counterpart moved verbatim into business/overview.md's existing Structure Convention section (an **Exceptions** sub-list), rather than a new section or a separate conventions.md note. templates/rules.md now points at that section by path instead of hardcoding the table.
rejected: A standalone 'Non-mirrored resources' section in overview.md; leaving the table in conventions.md instead.
why: The exception list carves exceptions out of the exact convention Structure Convention already states (business files mirror api/ 1:1); splitting the rule from its exceptions across two headers cuts against doc-philosophy's own one-fact-one-place principle. Unblocks the rules.md port (D045): project-specific resource names cannot live in a cinch template.

title: figma-restyle.md stays hand-authored — not ported as a cinch template
decision: Scoped out of the P1 template port. Its content (a per-component state-inventory methodology tied to a specific frontend/components/ tree, a worked example naming action-bar.md, and an assumed frontend/conventions.md § Documenting Complex Component States anchor) is project-specific enough that generalizing it would either lose the concrete guidance or require manifest keys (e.g. a frontend-component-docs path) serving only this one workflow. The check-frontend development.commands key, added in prep for this port, was reverted from both scaffold/manifest.example.yml and the project manifest since no other template needs it.
rejected: Porting it anyway with heavier genericization (prose-only component-inventory guidance, no path assumptions) — the resulting template would be thin enough to add little over the project keeping it as project-owned prose. Re-adding check-frontend speculatively for a possible future port — against D045's 'only what a template needs' contract.
why: D045's contract is that only what a template actually needs belongs in the scaffold's variable contract — check-frontend had exactly one prospective consumer, now none. Phase 1's roadmap exit line ('the project's workflows are rendered output') is revised to nine of ten; figma-restyle remains project-owned prose, the same status as any project doc with no portable procedure to extract.

title: P1: rules and doc-philosophy ported and rendering green; figma-restyle scoped out
decision: templates/rules.md and templates/doc-philosophy.md are authored as templates, rendered into project_deltadocs workflows/, and C2-green, verified individually (D033). rules.md's exception table moved to business/overview.md first (D052); doc-philosophy's stack-specific examples (Go/Svelte, session-vs-JWT, bcrypt/auth.go, .env.local, MCP-for-Svelte-docs) genericized into placeholder shapes per D045, preserving its concrete-vs-abstract contrast. figma-restyle.md was scoped out of the port entirely (D053) — nine of ten workflows are now rendered output; figma-restyle remains project-owned prose.
why: Completes the template-porting arc opened in E001-E003, closing HANDOFF's P1 blocker list except for the intentionally-excluded figma-restyle. Phase 1's roadmap exit line is revised accordingly.

title: The compaction anchor lives in task-primitive.md alone
decision: The anchor's content was added as a final cross-cutting section of templates/task-primitive.md (after the Completion ritual). execute-plan.md — the only workflow of the three that runs during task execution, where a mid-session compaction event is actually observable — gets one operational paragraph pointing at the section, not a restatement. plan-feature.md and fix-bug.md get compaction-anchor added to their existing "supplies unchanged" machinery name-lists, one word, no new prose.
rejected: Duplicating the anchor's contents into all three composing templates (a literal reading of D039's "each workflow template declares").
why: The literal reading directly conflicts with P2's own exit bar — no atomicity, manifest, or verification rule appears in more than one template — and the anchor is a cross-cutting epilogue citing backward, not a step in the planning or wrap-up sequence. Name-list additions match exactly how Atomicity/Context manifest/Verification tiers are already handled; only the workflow that runs during execution needs the operational signal.

title: P2 does not self-render the primitive into cinch's own repo
decision: The exit clause "cinch renders the primitive for its own use" is satisfied by the template existing, being C2-green in project_deltadocs, and being proven portable there — not by a self-manifest or self-render inside cinch's own repo, which stays out of scope until P3.
rejected: Building a minimal .agent/manifest.yml for cinch in P2 and rendering the primitive into cinch's own repo to literally satisfy the exit clause's wording.
why: D036's decision text says explicitly "From P3 onward, cinch plans with its own rendered task-primitive — it becomes the primitive's first consumer." Standing rule 2 says "P2 produces the primitive cinch then uses for P3 onward." fixtures/ (the actual cross-stack portability evidence, D017) is still empty, confirming that class of proof is P3/Wave-1 scope; building a second harness in P2 would produce nothing P3 consumes.

title: P2: compaction anchor added; plan-feature/fix-bug shrunk; execute-plan repointed
decision: templates/task-primitive.md gained the Compaction anchor section (D039). fix-bug.md's closing "differs from feature planning" parenthetical was deleted, not updated, and compaction-anchor added to its Phase 5 machinery list. plan-feature.md's Phase 3 shrank from five bullets restating primitive-section substance to a name-list plus the feature-specific persists-as-complete input. execute-plan.md's per-task step 4 now points at the primitive's Verification tiers instead of restating Tier 1/2/3, and Session Boundaries gained the compaction-reload paragraph. Each edit was verified individually before the next (D033): render into project_deltadocs, make check-harness C2 green, go test ./... D049 clean. Roadmap P2's exit line gained a parenthetical resolving the self-render ambiguity (D055); no self-render step ran against cinch's own repo.
why: Completes the roadmap's Phase 2 exit items: no atomicity, manifest, or verification rule appears in more than one template; fix-bug's differences note is deleted, not updated; the primitive now declares its compaction anchor, and the templates that compose it name it rather than duplicate it.

title: C6/C7 semantics: docs are the spec, code must conform; coverage warns; absent producers skip
decision: docs/INTROSPECTION.md defines the JSON contract both introspection producers must emit; checkTypes/checkRoutes implement C6/C7 in check.go. A type is documented by a ```go fence containing `type <Name> struct` (a models doc may document several types — signature.md does); a route by an `## METHOD /path` heading, with fences skipped (D046). Doc-upstream direction errors (a documented type/field/route must exist in the output); coverage direction warns (a real type/route with no doc). A repo that declares no introspect-types/introspect-routes key skips the corresponding check — same absence-is-a-declaration semantics as C5 and C12. Producers run with a 30s timeout. The consumer's RegisterRoutes signature became the RouteMux interface (http.ServeMux cannot enumerate its patterns) so the routes producer can record registrations at runtime (D028); this also fixed the code's mixed {id}/{tabID} registration for the same tab segment — the docs were consistent, the code was not, and the doc-upstream resolution was to make the code match the docs.
rejected: Matching a models doc to its H1 name only (signature.md documents two structs under ## X Struct headings and its H1 names neither); heading-level C6 without field parsing; coverage as an error (undocumented-but-legitimately-internal types like PendingSignatureIndicator and derivable liveness probes like GET /api/health would red the exit bar).
why: The doc is the spec, so a doc asserting a field or route that does not exist is a defect — that is the doc-upstream direction. Coverage is a question, not a verdict: the derivability gate (D012) says some code shapes should not be documented at all, and warn-level keeps the question visible without reddening check-harness (emit() returns success on warnings). The two standing project warnings — GET /api/health and PendingSignatureIndicator — are the designed answer: health has no contract to document, and the indicators type's contract lives in api prose.

title: C8's build ships with its P4.1 migration, not before
decision: Wave 3 stays blocked: no C8 code landed in P3 session 1. The rule-ID/marker migration is explicitly P4.1 scope (business docs today have numbered rules and no rule_prefix front-matter), and building the extraction machinery against a scheme no doc uses yet is speculative work D033 cannot verify — C8 has no real-repo referent until the migration runs. Roadmap P3's wave-3 bullet is annotated accordingly.
rejected: Implementing C8 vacuous-green (passes until P4.1 adds IDs): its forward direction is untestable against the real repo, and P3's exit bar does not require it — wave 3 is listed as blocked, not as an exit item.
why: D030 already calls wave 3 'a migration, not a build'. The checker is cheap; the migration is the work. Sequencing the build with the migration keeps every landed checker verified against a real repo at the moment it lands (D033).

title: Mechanical-audit closure: every mechanical audit in sync-docs/optimize-docs is already a checker; the rest is judgment, by design
decision: The P3 exit item closed by mapping each mechanical audit to an existing checker: doc-map regeneration after structure changes -> C1 (+ the pre-commit guard); stale markdown links -> C11; stale manifest paths bindings -> C4; stale command references in rendered workflows -> C2 (workflows are generated from {{vars}}, so a command reference cannot go stale without the render check firing). Two categories stay prose by design: sync-docs' commit-message greps (workaround/fix/issue...) are detection heuristics feeding judgment, not validations of a machine-readable fact (not doc-downstream, nothing to delete), and optimize-docs' 'manifest values restated as prose' audit is itself a deletion mandate (D009/D013), not a check. templates/optimize-docs.md's stale-references bullet was rewritten: dropped the harness-era 'skills' mention and now names C2/C4/C11 as the mechanical coverage, leaving the judgment residue explicit.
rejected: A new checker for backticked command references in hand-authored docs (noise: literal git/make invocations are not manifest keys, and rendered docs cannot go stale on commands); deleting the commit-message-grep guidance (it is a signal, not an audit).
why: The exit bar's intent is that no doc-side audit of a machine-readable fact remains a manual chore; that is true after this mapping. Adding a checker for the residual judgment classes would police prose the checkers cannot define.

title: Fixture repos: each is its own git repo; Go answers the full introspection contract, Node routes-only
decision: fixtures/go (toy Go service: model types with json tags, a route table registered through the RouteMux interface, both producers — a go/ast walk and a runtime recording-mux dump) and fixtures/node (toy Node service: dependency-free server with a central route table, the routes producer only). Each declares the same minimal .agent/ shape a real consumer must: all eleven template vars (paths.business is referenced 13x, so even the harness-less fixtures declare a business layer — overview.md plus two domain docs), seams (C12), test tiers with an e2e notes file. Each fixture is its own git repo so repoRoot() resolves to it (D042's empty-repo-marker precedent); `make fixtures` git-inits idempotently since CI checkouts cannot carry the nested .git (the outer repo tracks the fixture working trees and never the inner .git). Rendered workflows and index.md are committed in the outer repo; CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml) runs make test + make fixtures. Both fixtures check 'harness ok' — zero findings.
rejected: Fixture repos without own .git (cinch check resolves paths from the git root, so the fixture would be checked as the cinch repo — D042); giving the Node fixture a type producer (TS declaration emit is real work; D028 says repos may answer differently, and the fixture demonstrates exactly that asymmetry); letting the fixtures carry the project's health/indicators warnings (a fixture must be a clean gate).
why: D017's purpose is to fail loudly the moment a project-specific assumption survives into core; the fixtures exercise every wave-1 and wave-2 checker across two stacks. The route-table recording pattern (RouteMux + recording mux) mirrors the real consumer's refactor, so the fixture proves that pattern is portable, not just that it works once.

title: cinch renders its own harness: the primitive's first consumer
decision: cinch's own repo gained .agent/manifest.yml (harness_version pin, seams, test tiers, paths, commands bound honestly for a Go CLI — self-check, go test, go run, no fictional dev servers), .agent/business/overview.md (the bind is required by the shared templates; the absence of domain docs is the declaration that cinch has no business rules), and .agent/e2e.md. `cinch render` + `cinch index` + `cinch check` on cinch's own repo: 'harness ok'. The bound tests/ dir is real (tests/cli_test.go exercises the built binary — version show and self-check), and `make test`/`make fixtures` stay green.
rejected: A fictional business layer or dev-server commands to make the manifest look like a web project's (the portability question is whether the shared set renders honestly into a harness-less CLI repo — the answer is yes); leaving the self-harness for a later session (D036 says from P3 onward cinch plans with its own rendered primitive; D055 put the self-manifest in P3 scope).
why: This is the D036 promise landing: cinch is the task-primitive's first consumer, P4 sessions plan with .agent/workflows/plan-feature.md, and the self-check makes the harness guard its own repo.

title: P3 session 1: C6/C7 landed, fixtures green on two stacks, cinch self-harness live
decision: docs/INTROSPECTION.md defines the producer contract; checkTypes/checkRoutes ship in check.go with doc-upstream errors, coverage warns, and skip-when-absent semantics (D056). The consumer implemented both producers (go/ast types walk; runtime recording-mux route dump) and RegisterRoutes became the RouteMux interface; the code's mixed {id}/{tabID} tab-segment registration was fixed to match the docs. make check-harness is green in project_deltadocs with exactly two designed warnings (GET /api/health, PendingSignatureIndicator). fixtures/go and fixtures/node render and check 'harness ok' on every wave-1 and wave-2 checker; make fixtures git-inits each fixture repo; CI workflow added (dormant until O005). The mechanical-audit exit item is closed by mapping to existing checkers (D058) and optimize-docs' stale-references bullet rewritten. cinch rendered its own harness — .agent/manifest.yml, workflows, index — and checks itself 'harness ok' (D060); the bound tests/ dir holds a real CLI test. C8 stays deferred to P4.1 (D057).
why: Wave 2 landed and is verified against the real repo (D033) and both fixtures (D017); the P3 exit items are met except C8, which is blocked by design until the P4.1 migration. The self-harness completes D036's first-consumer promise.

title: Toy fixtures cut; real consumers are the portability test
decision: Delete fixtures/ and the fixtures make target. Portability is exercised by projectX (full-stack, domains, plans) and cinch itself (Go CLI, no domain layer). Portability is unproven until a third real consumer exists, and that gap is stated rather than papered over.
rejected: Maintaining a toy Go repo and a toy Node repo in CI.
why: A fixture proves cinch renders into a repo shaped like a fixture. It catches hardcoded paths; it cannot catch a template assuming a workflow structure only projectX has, because a toy repo has no structure to conflict with. Confirmed empirically: rendering into cinch surfaced invented manifest bindings, hardcoded tests/handlers and tests/models in check-rules, and dangling .agent/ references — and a fixture would have passed all of it, because we would have given it a business/ and an api/ to make the render succeed. Meanwhile two synthetic repos must stay valid as the schema evolves or CI reddens for unrelated reasons. False assurance is worse than an acknowledged gap.

title: business/ becomes domain/ across both consumers
decision: Rename the rules directory and its binding to `domain/` / `paths.domain` in cinch and project_deltadocs as one change: templates, both manifests, both directories, C5's key, and the `business/<domain>.md` path literal in D010. cinch's placeholder `overview.md` is rewritten as a real domain layer — overview plus per-domain rule file with IDs, per the §7.3 guardrail.
rejected: `rules/` — literal, but collides with the `rules.md` workflow name in paths and in file lists; `invariants/` — accurate but reads heavy in an app repo.
why: The audit (§7) showed the name produced a wrong answer: 'does this repo have business rules?' gets a no from a CLI, while 'does this repo have domain rules?' gets a yes — cinch's domain is rendering, checking, and templating, with several rules already enforced by tests. `domain/` generalises cleanly across consumer shapes and makes the C8 / `// cinch:rule` closure applicable to a second genuinely different-shaped consumer, the portability evidence a toy could not produce (D040). Planned as one change because C4/C5 validate bindings against the filesystem and D005 fails the render on an undefined key — whichever consumer lags breaks its own check or render.

title: Templates vary by file-level selection; fragments compose when variance bites
decision: The renderer selects whole template files from manifest key absence — a template declaring `requires:` front-matter is skipped when that key is absent. Fragments are separate template files with their own `requires:` keys, composed into the base at an anchor; inclusion is a file list, so substitution stays literal (D005). Applied now: fix-bug's dev-server/troubleshooting rows and check-rules' API/model classification become fragments; `paths.tests` gains optional `handlers`/`models` sub-keys for the classification. Future fragments one template at a time as variance bites (sync-docs routing table, task-primitive example manifests).
rejected: Conditionals in the substituter — cheapest now, but branching in files the runtime model reads breaks D005. Fragments wholesale before any template's variance has bitten — speculative.
why: Whole-workflow applicability is a file-list property, not a substitution property. The audit's §1.3 and §1.4 findings are both a checker that permits absence (C5) plus a template that assumes presence — selection resolves the disagreement by data, not by branching. Two fragments bite in this session's cleanups already: fix-bug's dev-server row references commands cinch must not declare, and check-rules' classification is project_deltadocs' taxonomy. The no-domain path has no real consumer yet; the gap is stated, not papered over (D040).

title: C8 semantics: rule IDs are doc-side data; forward coverage warns, reverse stale claims error; cinch:ignore declares exemptions
decision: C8 (rule.go) reads rule IDs from the docs themselves: rule_prefix front-matter plus a bold **PREFIX-NNN** token at the start of each numbered item in a non-overview domain doc. IDs are permanent and never reused (R5, enforced by TestRuleIDsUnique). Forward direction — a rule with no `// cinch:rule <ID>` marker — warns: coverage is a question, and future-decision constraints (harness.md HARNESS-001) are untestable by design (guardrail §7.3). Reverse — a marker resolving to no rule — errors: a stale marker is a false checkmark, the worst failure mode in the loop (D027). A rule both marked and ignored errors; an ignore naming a nonexistent rule errors; a rule doc with numbered items but no rule_prefix errors (pre-migration). The marker scan reads the source tree only — documentation surfaces (.agent/, templates/, docs/, decisions.jsonl) and artifacts (.git/, bin/) are skipped, because D027's own example token lives in the append-only log forever. Untestable rules declare `<!-- cinch:ignore <ID> -->` under the rule item and drop out of the coverage question; `cinch ignores` lists the inventory for the check-rules/optimize-docs audits. The user chose warn-over-error for forward and markers-above-enforcing-functions for checker-enforced rules (C2/C12 markers sit above checkRendered/checkSeams).
rejected: Forward as error with an in-doc exemption marker (the roadmap's literal exit bar, but it would duplicate check-rules' semantic N/A classification and red cinch's own untestable R1); scanning the whole tree including docs (the append-only decisions.jsonl would perpetually false-positive D027's example token); requiring behavior tests for every checker-enforced rule (markers above the enforcing function give the same self-correcting deletion semantics at zero ceremony).
why: The marker is a comment token, so core stays agnostic (D003); the doc is the declaration (D027), so the ID scheme is data, not a registry. Warn-forward matches D056's coverage-warns precedent and keeps check-harness green with the untestable residue declared by cinch:ignore. Error-reverse is the one place a false positive is unforgivable. Landing the build with the migration (D057) gave every behavior a real-repo referent on day one (D033).

title: C10 semantics: lateral diff-coupling at the working-tree boundary; a change touching a domain's owns: paths without its domain doc warns
decision: C10 (diff.go, checkDiffCoupling) is the mechanism D012 reserves for the semantic residue: a behaviour change that falsifies a rule's text without updating it. Boundary is the working tree vs HEAD (git diff HEAD --name-only — index and worktree both, so the question is asked before the commit is made, at the moment the answer is cheapest, and self-corrects when code and doc land in the same change). A change touching any path under a domain's owns: front-matter list but not that domain's doc warns once per domain (changed paths named, not one warn per path). Warn-level per the roadmap: most commits legitimately don't change rules. Skip silently when not a git repo, when HEAD does not exist, when the git binary is missing, or when no domain layer or owns: lists are declared — the same absence-is-a-declaration semantics as C5/C6/C7/C12. On a clean tree the diff is empty, so existing exit bars (cinch self-check, project check-harness) are untouched.
rejected: Per-commit semantics (git show HEAD: the question is asked after the commit when the answer is more expensive, and a multi-commit feature only surfaces on its last commit); a range flag (--commits N / -since: flag surface on a no-flag CLI for a warn-level question); wiring into the pre-commit hook (harness-side glue per D024 — the hook shell calls the binary and nothing else; the guard's job is making check-harness itself ask the question).
why: D009 classifies it as lateral: it binds a change set (an authored artifact) to the domain doc and validates no doc's copy of a machine-readable fact, so nothing duplicated gets policed instead of deleted. Git as a subprocess matches the compiled-in-checker design (D024) — the runIntrospection precedent already shells out under a timeout. The working-tree boundary is the only one that fires when the answer is cheap and stays silent on a clean tree; per-commit semantics would also miss renames and squashed history.

title: P4.2: C10 diff-coupling landed — D065 decision, diff.go, hermetic git fixture tests
decision: D065 logs C10 as the D012 semantic-residue mechanism, lateral under D009, with a working-tree boundary (git diff HEAD --name-only — index and worktree, question asked pre-commit, self-correcting when code and doc land in the same change, silent on clean trees). checkDiffCoupling in diff.go reads owns: front-matter lists (ownsList, extended parseDomainDoc in rule.go), matches changed paths exactly or by directory prefix (trailing slash normalized), and warns once per domain when that domain's doc is not part of the change. Skips silently when not a git repo, when HEAD is unborn, or when no domain layer/owns are declared — absence-is-a-declaration, same as C5/C6/C7/C12. The git subprocess runs under a 10s timeout, consistent with runIntrospection (D024). 12 unit tests cover the parser and boundary semantics against hermetic fixture repos (GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null); cinch's own harness.md owns list grew rule.go/diff.go/introspect.go so the harness domain names its whole checker layer.
why: C10 is the last cinch-side P4 item, and the handoff's 'worth a decision entry on direction before building' is answered by D065. Verified against both real consumers: cinch self-check exit 0 with the two known C11 warns; project check-harness exit 0 unchanged; a scratch content change to backend/handlers/tab.go in project_deltadocs fired one C10 warn per owning domain (signatures, tabs) and reverted clean. During the session the self-check itself asked the C10 question about the uncommitted check.go change — the designed behavior: warn-level, answer was 'no harness rule changed', and the owns-list update (same change) resolved it.

title: The admission test is a two-question gate; the pruning pass removes and carves out the residue
decision: doc-philosophy.md gains 'The Admission Test' at its head: before writing, ask *can an agent recover this by reading the source?* If yes, it is not written — point at the source instead. If no, ask *could a code change falsify this?* If yes, it is a business rule: it belongs in domain/<domain>.md with a rule ID (C8/C10-guarded), not prose. If no, it is a decision or a why: prose. optimize-docs.md gains a prune-first step applying the test retroactively: gate-failing content is removed — not trimmed, not refreshed — and the fix step makes removal the default. Two carve-outs survive the pass: domain/ rule docs (the non-derivable residue D012 reserves) and generated workflows (C2-owned). A removal must be spot-checked recoverable from source (search before committing), and the checkers plus the index re-run after pruning.
rejected: A single-question gate without residue routing (D012's semantic residue left without an address); a refresh-and-trim pass applying the gate to new content only (violates D013's retroactive mandate); letting the pass touch domain/ rule docs (contradicts D064/C8/C10 — the residue is guarded, not pruned).
why: D012 names the gate and the residue but not where residue content goes or what survives a retroactive prune; D013 mandates removal but not its safety discipline. The gate's second question routes the residue to the one surface that already guards it (rule IDs + C10), and the carve-outs keep the pruning pass from eating the semantic layer it exists to protect. The recoverability spot-check is what makes deletion honest: remove only what source can still answer.

title: The coverage audit enumerates by script, not by hand; seam allowances are declared command-id lists validated by C12

A declaration gates nothing by itself: enforcement is per-harness glue, and the first piece is the project's opencode auditor agent (read-only, task-denied, bash restricted to the checker commands).
rejected: Keeping hand enumeration as the audit's step 1 (D014 says enumeration is no-model work — a hand extraction can silently drop a rule the checker never misses); allowances as free-form capabilities (not resolvable against the manifest, not enforceable by any harness); enforcement glue in cinch templates (per-harness by definition, D024).
why: D014's Auditor seam is strong-model verification over a script-produced list — the template previously had the model produce the list itself, the exact seam design C8 rendered obsolete. The manifest binding keeps the template portable; C3-style resolution catches a typo that would silently widen or narrow a seam. The glue stays consumer-side where harnesses live.

title: Claude Code seam enforcement is an agent envelope plus a manifest-derived PreToolUse guard
decision: The auditor seam's Claude Code half landed in project_deltadocs: .claude/agents/auditor.md (tools: Read/Grep/Glob/Bash — no Edit/Write/Agent — body mirroring the opencode agent) with an agent-scoped PreToolUse hook running .claude/hooks/auditor-bash-guard.py. The guard reads the hook JSON, resolves seams.auditor.allow ids to command literals through development.commands at runtime (quoted and unquoted literal shapes, inline comments), auto-allows a matching command via permissionDecision only when its remainder is free of chaining/expansion characters (; | & ` $ and control chars), and otherwise exits 2 (deny), failing closed when the manifest is unreadable, the seam has no allow list, or no id resolves. The check-rules skill entry points now route the audit to the auditor agent in both harnesses. The stale-path pass was narrower than the P5 handoff believed: only the check-rules and rules skills (.claude) and rules (.opencode) plus AGENTS.md carried the pre-P4 .agent/business/ path; plan-feature/fix-bug/optimize-docs/sync-docs skills were already clean.
rejected: A static mirror of the opencode envelope's make patterns in the agent file or in settings deny rules — the allowance is data with a resolution contract, a hardcoded copy is exactly the drift the D067 handoff's live-property note warns about, and settings-file rules are session-wide, not seam-scoped; a project-settings-level PreToolUse hook — it cannot distinguish which agent is running, so it would widen every session.
why: The opencode envelope (D067) is static by platform necessity; Claude Code agent-scoped hooks make enforcement derivable from the manifest itself, so adding an id to seams.auditor.allow now widens the Claude Code seam with no glue edit — declaration is enforcement here rather than duplicated elsewhere. Fail-closed keeps a parse regression from silently opening the envelope. The guard is deliberately tighter than the opencode pattern envelope (exact literals, so the project's make check* superset does not leak check-frontend/check-backend into the auditor), an asymmetry to revisit when a third harness appears. Known gap, deferred: the check-rules template references `cinch ignores` with no manifest binding and no envelope allowance in either harness; the N/A inventory remains derivable by reading the cinch:ignore markers in the domain docs.

title: check-rules step 3 hardens: trust the closure before declaring a rule unmarked
decision: The first interactive project-side audit (E017) misreported PERM-004 as unmarked under a zero-unmarked C8 closure: the marker existed (backend/tests/handlers/actionbar_states_test.go, above TestSignOnlyPermission_CanSignButNotEdit) but sat in a UI-state test file outside permissions.md's owns: paths, so the semantic pass never read it — and the report suspected C8's wiring instead of its own file set. templates/check-rules.md step 3 now instructs: a gap under a zero-unmarked closure is by definition not a missing marker — search the tree for the rule's marker first and judge the quality of the marker's test instead. Renders into both consumers (re-rendered in cinch and project_deltadocs, C2 green).
rejected: Adding owns:-path-driven marker discovery to the workflow (the checker's closure is already authoritative; the fix belongs where the misdiagnosis happened — step 3's gap framing); amending C8 (correctly wired — the audit's zero-unmarked output was true, and the gap was marker quality, not marker existence).
why: The misdiagnosis is the class of error the seam's semantic half must not make — it undercut its own report by doubting the mechanical closure (D067: the checkers never miss a rule; a hand extraction can). The amendment keeps the checker authoritative and makes the semantic half judge marker quality, not marker existence.

title: P5.6: project-side interactive Claude Code audit ran — PERM-004 gap closed, step 3 hardened (D073)
decision: The last unverified path executed: a fresh interactive Claude Code session in project_deltadocs ran /check-rules with the auditor agent — guard auto-allowed make check-harness / make ignores, and a probe denial (tail on the events log) confirmed live enforcement project-side. Closure: zero C8 findings, ignores = CAT-003 + MEMB-006. Semantic half over all rules: 64 testable covered, PERM-004 under-enforced — 'sign grants read but not edit' had no route-level coverage (the read-access clause untested entirely) and its marker sat above a resolver-mapping test (TestSignOnlyPermission_CanSignButNotEdit, outside permissions.md owns: paths). Backend go test green; both consumers' cinch check exit 0 (project: 2 known C6/C7 + 2 designed C10 questions on the uncommitted diff; cinch: 2 known C11 + 1 designed C10 question; all clear on commit).
why: Completes the P5 seam's last unverified path — the audit executed interactively end-to-end (closure → classification → report → proposal → executor-apply) in the Claude Code consumer, and its one real gap (the read-access clause) is closed while its one misfire (unmarked claim) became a workflow hardening.

title: docs/ holds spec, contract, and plan+status only; historical artifacts are deleted
decision: docs/ is the core/philosophy namespace: PHILOSOPHY.md (spec), INTROSPECTION.md (contract), ROADMAP.md (plan+status). Historical artifacts — RATIONALE.md (superseded by ROADMAP's landed phases), FINDINGS-render-audit.md (P1-era worklist), HANDOFF.md (session state), decisions-log.md (a doc-downstream copy of the consumer's events-log schema) — are deleted; git is the archive. Session handoffs live in plan files and events, never docs/.
rejected: Keeping the four as living docs; a docs/operational/ subdirectory (docs/ is the core namespace — ops/ is the sibling folder for how-this-repo-runs, per D044).
why: The derivability gate applied to cinch's own docs (D012's 'apply this to the harness itself'): each artifact fails it on its own term — RATIONALE is a stale snapshot of phases now marked [landed], FINDINGS is a resolved worklist, HANDOFF is point-in-time session state, and decisions-log validates a doc's copy of a machine-readable schema, the exact duplication the direction rule forbids (D009). The taxonomy gives sessions a stable namespace: spec, contract, plan+status, nothing else.

title: C13 is retired from the checker numbering — it is a unit test, not a checker
decision: No C13. The template-purity check is the unit test TestTemplatePurity (templates_test.go), never a C-number; a retired C-number stays retired, the permanence spirit of HARNESS-005 applied to the numbering. The checker registry lists C1–C12 only; prose cites the test name, not the number (stragglers fixed in Phase 3).
rejected: Keeping 'C13' as the repo's house name for the purity test (the E016 usage); renumbering the checkers to reclaim the slot.
why: TestTemplatePurity validates cinch's own source, not a consumer's rendered/bound state — outside the C1–C12 check layer by definition (D049), which is exactly why a checker registry that listed it would lie about the layer's scope. The numbering stays stable so registry rows, harness rules, and decision refs keep one meaning per number.

title: Go layout: one binary, one checker package, internal/ split
decision: Phase 3 layout: cmd/cinch/main.go (usage, dispatch, repoRoot/agentDir); internal/manifest/, internal/render/, internal/index/, internal/check/ (C1–C7, C9, C11, C12 in check.go, C8 in rule.go, C10 in diff.go, plus introspect.go and report.go), internal/version/; version/ generated store untouched; tests/cli_test.go unchanged. Makefile builds ./cmd/cinch to bin/cinch, so binary-relative templatesDir/versionDir resolution is untouched.
rejected: Eight checker packages; keeping the root-level chronology grouping.
why: One checker package: C8/C10 share report and helpers, and splitting further is churn-for-ceremony. The split groups by concept, not chronology — the point of the reorg. The plan's single layout sketch is logged up front so Phase 3's file moves are mechanical rather than a second design pass.
